Whomsoever
hoom-so-EV-er
pron.
From whom, so and ever: whatever person, without restriction. Webster 1828: any person whatever. In the book of Daniel it is the word on which the doctrine of God’s rule over kingdoms turns.

Biblical Definition

Twice in one chapter, and both times as the lesson Nebuchadnezzar must learn by losing his reason, Daniel states the government of the world: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men (Daniel 4:17), and again, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will (Daniel 4:25). The clause is unqualified. Not permits, not influences — giveth it to whomsoever he will, and the appended phrase about setting up the basest of men forecloses the objection that God only gives thrones to the deserving. Our Lord uses the same word of the sovereign disclosure of the Father: no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him (Matthew 11:27). Knowledge of God is a gift in the Son’s giving. Even the devil, offering the kingdoms of the world, borrows the construction: to whomsoever I will I give it (Luke 4:6) — a claim the Lord does not stop to dispute, because Daniel has already settled whose it is.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WHOMSOEVER as the objective case of whosoever — any person whatever; whatever person, without limitation or exception.

expand to see more

WHOMSOEVER, pron. — The objective case of whosoever.

Any person whatever; whatever person.

Compare WHOSOEVER, whatever person; WHATSOEVER, whatever thing.

The -soever ending generalizes without exception, and is one of the marks of the Authorized Version’s precision.

From whom, so, and ever.

Key Scripture

Daniel 4:17 — "This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men."

Daniel 4:25 — "That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will."

Matthew 11:27 — "All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him."

Luke 4:6 — "And the devil said unto him, All this power will I give thee, and the glory of them: for that is delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it."

Modern Corruption

Daniel 4 states God’s absolute disposal of thrones without a qualifying clause, and Matthew 11:27 states the same absoluteness about the knowledge of God — both are routinely softened into permission.

expand to see more

The most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. The sentence has no escape hatch, and Daniel adds the hardest part: and setteth up over it the basest of men. God’s government of history is not confined to the rise of good rulers, and any doctrine of providence that quietly restricts it to what we would have chosen has stopped reading mid-verse. Romans 13:1 states the same thing for the New Testament church living under Nero: there is no power but of God, the powers that be are ordained of God. This does not sanctify what wicked rulers do — Scripture judges them without hesitation, and the doctrine of the lesser magistrate provides for lawful resistance — but it denies that any throne is held outside God’s disposal. Nebuchadnezzar had to lose his reason to learn it, and the text says he was restored the moment he lifted his eyes to heaven.

Matthew 11:27 applies the same unqualified sovereignty to the knowledge of God, and it is the harder of the two for the modern hearer. No man knows the Father save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him. Knowledge of God is not the achievement of the seeker but the gift of the Revealer, which is the doctrine of effectual calling stated by Christ Himself — and it stands immediately before the freest invitation in the Gospels, Come unto me, all ye that labour. Scripture sets sovereign election and universal invitation side by side in adjoining verses without embarrassment, and the systems that must remove one to keep the other — whether by making election conditional on foreseen faith or by muting the free offer — are tidier than the text.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic man di, whoever; Greek hos ean and hos an, whoever, whomsoever; the -soever ending renders the generalizing particle in both languages.

expand to see more

Aramaic man di yitsbe — whom he will; the clause of Daniel 4:17 and 4:25, unqualified in the original.

Aramaic illay (H5943) — the Most High; the title under which God’s rule over kingdoms is asserted in Daniel 4.

Greek hos ean — whoever, whomsoever; the generalizing relative of Matthew 11:27 and Luke 4:6.

Greek apokalupto (G601) — to uncover, to reveal; the Son’s act in Matthew 11:27.

Greek boulomai (G1014) — to will, to purpose; the verb of the Son’s sovereign choice in the same verse.

Usage

"Giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men (Daniel 4:17) — the clause has no escape hatch."

"He to whomsoever the Son will reveal him (Matthew 11:27) — knowledge of God is a gift in the Son’s giving."

"To whomsoever I will I give it (Luke 4:6) — even the tempter borrows the construction; Daniel has settled whose it is."
